volumes.title: Hannah's Half
volumes.text:
My grandmother Hannah Ashby played one air on the fiddle better than anyone in Emberwick, and she only ever played the first half of it. It is in D, slow, three beats to the bar: eight bars that climb from the open D string to a high A and hang there. Then she would stop and lay the fiddle down.

“The second half went over the fells with a man who never brought it back,” she said, and would say no more.

She left me the fiddle and the half tune. I am Corwin Ashby, and I play for dances and for my supper. This spring I mean to walk the country round with a book of ruled paper, write down whatever airs I am given, and ask everywhere for the rest of Hannah's. A tune that stops in mid-air keeps a man awake.

volumes.title: The Sluice at Harrowmill
volumes.text:
A day's walk up the river Ember from Emberwick stands Harrowmill, where the miller's wife, Bess Tranter, plays a jig that copies the mill. It is in G, six quick beats to the bar. The low strain thumps along on the two bottom strings like the wheel turning. The high strain runs in a stream of short notes, like water let through the sluice.

She plays it with small bows near the tip and a lift on the first note of every three, so that it bounces. Her father made it while waiting for corn to grind, and always claimed the mill wrote it.

I played her my grandmother's half air and asked if she knew the rest. She did not. But she said the way it hangs on its last note sounded like fell-country playing. They leave notes hanging up there, like washing.

volumes.title: Old Tam's Gate
volumes.text:
On a farm outside Netherby, in the Lowlands, I met Tam Oakes, a ploughman of eighty, who plays one slow air and plays it leaning on the same gate every evening. The tune has taken the gate's name.

It is in A, but with the G left natural, which gives it a grey, old-fashioned sound. He takes a whole bar to each bow and slides up to the high C rather than stepping there. He had it from a travelling tinker, who said he had it from a dream. I wrote it down by the last of the light.

Then I played him my grandmother Hannah's half tune, the one I am walking the country to finish. He listened twice with his eyes shut. He had heard it once, he said, whole, at a hiring fair sixty years ago. A fell man played it, on a dark fiddle.

volumes.title: Goose Fair Morning
volumes.text:
At Withy Cross, in the Lowlands, the Goose Fair is opened each year by the three Dunnock sisters playing a reel of the same name. It is in D and goes at a gallop.

The trick of it is in the bow, which rocks between the D string and the A so that an open string is always ringing under the tune. From across the green it sounds remarkably like geese. Before each strong beat there is a cut, a flick of the third finger too quick to count as a note. Two sisters play the tune together. The eldest drops to a drone when her arm tires.

I am Corwin Ashby, collecting airs and looking for the lost half of one. I played it to the sisters between sets. They had never heard it, were too busy to care, and bought me a pie. Not every road has a signpost.

volumes.title: Low Fen Lights
volumes.text:
Silas Wend cuts reeds in the marsh east of Emberwick and plays his fiddle with a wooden clothes peg clipped to the bridge. The peg mutes it to a murmur, so the sound will not carry over the water and put up the wildfowl.

His one air is in E minor and has no steady beat. Each phrase lasts as long as a slow breath and then waits. He calls it after the pale lights that are seen over the fen on still nights. He taught it to me by ear, a phrase at a time, sitting in his punt. Paper does not last in the marsh.

I played him my grandmother's unfinished air. “That's a tune with the door left open,” he said. He could not close it. But the fell fiddlers come down to the Grey Coast each autumn to sell wool, and I might ask there.

volumes.title: Herring Lamps
volumes.text:
At Skarne Haven on the Grey Coast, Meg Corrie plays on the quay outside the net loft, with the fiddle held low against her arm instead of under her chin, so that she can call to the boats without stopping.

Her tune is named for the lamps the herring boats hang out at night. It is in G and moves long-short, long-short, like a hull on a swell. Under it she keeps the open D string droning, a second voice that never changes its mind.

I am Corwin Ashby of Emberwick, and I had come to ask the fell wool-sellers about the lost half of my grandmother's air. They had been and gone. But Meg knew my eight bars at once. “That's the front of Garth's tune,” she said. “Josiah Garth, of Skerrow in the Fells. He only has the back.”

volumes.title: The Net-Mender's Waltz
volumes.text:
Three days of rain kept me in the net loft at Skarne Haven, on the Grey Coast, with an old net-mender called Dan Pellow. Dan cannot play a note. He hums.

What he hums is a waltz in D, three beats to the bar, with the second beat a shade late. It goes exactly with his hands: pull, knot, pull. He has hummed it at his work for fifty years and never thought it worth a name. I put it on the fiddle for him, and he corrected me by tapping my knee whenever I hurried.

A tune can live a long while in someone with no instrument at all. I wrote it in my book as his. When the rain eased I shouldered my fiddle and turned north for Skerrow, where a man named Garth is said to keep the other half of my grandmother's air.

volumes.title: Cold Shoulder Pass
volumes.text:
The road into the Northern Fells goes over Cold Shoulder Pass, and there is a stone hut at the top where drovers sleep. I shared it with one, Abel Rudd, and his fiddle.

Abel plays a striding air in A that the drovers use to keep cattle moving. For it he retunes the two low strings a note higher, so the fiddle is tuned A, E, A, E. Every open string then rings along with the tune, and the instrument sounds twice its size. Fell tuning, he calls it. He retuned mine without asking.

I told him I was Corwin Ashby, walking to Skerrow to find Josiah Garth and the lost half of an air. He was quiet a while. Old Garth died in the winter, he said, at ninety-one. But Skerrow was a day further on, and I had come too far to turn back.

volumes.title: Three Sheep Short
volumes.text:
I reached Skerrow farm, high in the Northern Fells, on the day of the shearing, and was handed a plate before I could explain myself.

The shearers' own tune is a jig in D called Three Sheep Short. It has three strains, and the third stops two bars early, on purpose. Every stranger who dances to it takes two more steps and falls over somebody. The whole barn then shouts the count. Six fiddles play it at once, roughly, with a great deal of foot.

When I had fallen over twice I asked Josiah Garth's son about his late father's half tune, the answer to my grandmother's. He is a shepherd and does not play. “Father taught that to one person only,” he said. “My girl Ellen.” I asked where Ellen was. He pointed south, the way I had come. “Married a baker.”

volumes.title: Garth's Ewe
volumes.text:
At Skerrow, in the Northern Fells, the shepherd Thomas Garth could not give me the tune I had walked a month to find. He gave me another, and a story.

The tune is a slow air in G that his father Josiah made for a favourite ewe. Thomas whistled it and I wrote it down, with the dog howling the long notes. Its phrases all come downhill. They settle where another tune would climb.

The story is this. As a young man Josiah walked south to a hiring fair and met a girl with a fiddle. They made an air between them, she the first half and he the second. He went home for lambing, meaning to return. Snow shut the pass, and then life got in the way. Her name was Hannah. And his granddaughter Ellen, who has his half, married a baker in Emberwick.

volumes.title: Coming Down by Skerrow
volumes.text:
Walking home from the Northern Fells to Emberwick took me three days, and somewhere on the first of them I began, for the first time in my life, to make an air of my own.

It is in D and goes at walking pace, because my feet wrote most of it. I can hear where the rest came from. The thump in the low strain is the mill at Harrowmill. The drone is Meg Corrie's from the coast. The last note of each phrase hangs, fell fashion. A tune built from other tunes should say so, and I have put their names in the margin.

My book now holds eleven airs and half of another. As for the baker's wife, one of Emberwick's bakeries is in Mill Street, two streets from my door. I have bought bread there for six years, from a woman with a northern voice.

volumes.title: The Whole Air
volumes.text:
Ellen Dobbs, who was Ellen Garth, came to the back door of the Mill Street bakery in Emberwick with flour to her elbows. I played her my grandmother Hannah's eight bars and stopped on the high A, where Hannah always stopped.

Ellen wiped her hands, took my fiddle and played eight more. They come down from that A by the same steps the first half climbed, turn once, and settle on the open D like a door closing quietly. Her grandfather Josiah called it the Answer. He never had the front.

We played it whole among the cooling loaves, a half each, then changed about. It is the twelfth air in my book, with two names over it: Hannah Ashby and Josiah Garth. I walked to the Fells and back for a tune that was two streets away. I sleep very well now.

volumes.title: January: The Dumb D
volumes.text:
I am Lettice Corran, and for eleven years I have played the organ in the chapel on Tallow Street, Emberwick. It has two keyboards, a row of pedals, eleven stops and one silence. On the principal stop, the D just above the middle of the keyboard has never spoken. Press it and you get a sigh of wind and nothing more.

In January the chapel is so cold that the ivory keys bite, and I play in mittens with the ends cut off. Cold flattens the pipes as well, so the whole organ sinks a little below the choir, who blame each other.

I have learned to play around the D as one walks round a puddle, borrowing the note from the flute stop or leaving a hole and hoping. Most Sundays nobody notices. I notice.

volumes.title: February: Dickon at the Bellows
volumes.text:
An organ breathes, and ours in the Tallow Street chapel at Emberwick breathes by hand. Behind the case is a long ash handle, and on the end of it is Dickon Pyle, aged twelve, who pumps for a small fee and a seat near the stove.

A lead weight on a string shows him how full the bellows are. If it climbs past the chalk mark the wind is running out, and the whole organ sags in pitch like a tired singer. For a loud piece he must pump like a man bailing a boat, so I knock once on the case to warn him.

The bellows leather is cracked along the folds. In a quiet passage you can hear it hiss. It wants replacing, and the pipes want a tuner, and the chapel has afforded neither in eleven years. I have put a jar on the vestry shelf.

volumes.title: March: What the Stops Do
volumes.text:
Each stop knob on an organ brings on one rank of pipes, a pipe for every key. On the chapel organ at Emberwick, which I play, the principal is the plain strong voice, a row of open metal pipes. The flute is wooden and stopped with a plug, which makes it soft and round and an octave deeper than its length would suggest. The trumpet has a brass tongue that buzzes. It is kept for weddings and last verses.

Draw several stops and the voices add together. That is all the mystery there is.

March is the damp month. The wooden sliders swell, and a stop that came out with one finger in January wants both hands. The trackers, the thin rods that join each key to its pipe, swell too, and the keys feel like pressing into porridge. One plays gently in March, and forgives.

volumes.title: April: Walking the Bride In
volumes.text:
Prudence Hale married the ferryman this month, in the chapel on Tallow Street, and I played her up the aisle.

The art of a wedding is not the tune but the length. A bride takes about forty seconds to walk our aisle, fewer if she is nervous, and the organist must reach the last chord just as she reaches the front. So I play a march of my own making, built in four-bar pieces, any of which can be repeated or left out. It opens and shuts like a telescope.

This bride stopped halfway to see to her shoe. I went round the middle piece three times and nobody knew. The march is in D, and its grandest note is the one D that has never sounded on our principal stop. I gave it to the trumpet instead. The ferryman wept. I take no credit.

volumes.title: May: Giving the Note
volumes.text:
The choir of the Tallow Street chapel in Emberwick practises on Thursdays, fourteen voices and one organist, with the windows open and a blackbird outside competing with the trebles.

My humblest duty is to give the note: one soft chord, so that everyone begins in the same place. After that the secret is to lead by a hair. Organ pipes speak a little late, and sound takes its time crossing a room. An organist who follows the choir drags it slower and slower until the whole company comes to a stop, looking hurt.

The other May skill is filling in. When the collection outlasts the music, I take the last line of the tune, turn it upside down, wander about on the flute stop, and come home as the plates reach the back. Nobody has ever remarked on it. That is how I know it is going well.

volumes.title: June: Sour Trumpets
volumes.text:
Heat untunes an organ in a particular way. As the air warms, the ordinary pipes rise in pitch. The reed pipes hardly move. So the trumpet stop, which agreed with everything in April, sounds sour against the rest by midsummer. There is no cure but a tuner or a cool day. I leave the trumpet pushed in and let the principal carry the chapel, hole and all.

Dickon Pyle pumps the bellows in his shirtsleeves, and in June I pay him partly in ginger beer.

The jar on the vestry shelf now holds about a third of a tuner. Old Mr. Elias Thrupp, who was organist at Emberwick for forty years before me, is said to have tuned the organ himself. He is also said to have quarrelled with the committee over playing music nobody had asked for. I think I should have liked him.

volumes.title: July: A Cipher in the Sermon
volumes.text:
A cipher is a note that sounds by itself and will not stop, because the little valve under its pipe has stuck open. In July, in the middle of the sermon, a low F sharp on the flute stop began to hoot softly, like an owl with something on its mind.

I pushed the flute stop in, which silenced it, and knocked twice on the case to tell Dickon to stop pumping. Dickon had dozed off, woke at the knock, and pumped harder.

Afterwards I crawled inside the organ with a candle, my first time in eleven years as organist here in Emberwick. A dead moth lay on the valve. While I was there I found the dumb D standing in its row, looking just like its neighbours. I did not dare lift it. Pipe metal is as soft as cheese and dents under a thumb.

volumes.title: August: Pedals in Stockinged Feet
volumes.text:
August is the quiet month at the Tallow Street chapel, with half of Emberwick in the fields, and I use it to practise the pedals.

The pedals are a keyboard for the feet, a row of long wooden levers that play the deepest pipes, some of them twice the height of a man. One plays in stockinged feet, toe and heel, knees together, finding the notes by feel. Looking down is fatal.

I also taught Dickon Pyle, who pumps the bellows, to pick out a tune on the keys. He is quick. A blower who knows what the music is about to do can pump ahead of it. In return he let me try the handle. It is far harder than it looks, and I lasted one verse. Each of us now thinks rather more of the other.

volumes.title: September: The Harvest Supper
volumes.text:
The harvest supper in the chapel hall at Emberwick was held this year for the organ, which needs a tuner and new bellows leather and has had neither in my eleven years.

I played for the singing: plain strong tunes that everyone knows, on the principal and the flute, with the trumpet added for the last verse now that cooler weather has brought it back into agreement. There were pies, an auction of apples, and a marrow raffled twice by mistake.

We counted the money in the vestry. With the jar, it comes to the cost of the tuner and the leather, and fourpence over. I wrote that night to Mr. Halloran Pym of Netherby. Dickon, my bellows boy, asked whether a tuner can mend the D that has never spoken. I told him the truth, which is that I do not know.

volumes.title: October: Mr. Pym Listens
volumes.text:
Mr. Halloran Pym, organ tuner, spent three days inside the chapel organ at Emberwick. He sets one rank of pipes true and then tunes every other pipe against it, listening for the beats, the slow wah-wah two notes make when they almost agree. As they come together the beats slow, and when they vanish the pipe is right. He taps a brass cone into a pipe's top to sharpen it, or over the top to flatten it.

On the second day he reached the D that has been dumb for as long as I, Lettice Corran, have played here. He lifted the pipe out, looked down it, and drew out a tight roll of paper.

It was music, handwritten. For Midwinter. E. Thrupp. Hidden from the committee. Whoever finds this, play it. He set the pipe back. I pressed the key, and the D spoke.

volumes.title: November: Learning Mr. Thrupp
volumes.text:
The music found rolled inside our dumb organ pipe is three pages long, in the hand of Elias Thrupp, who played at Emberwick before me. I have practised it every evening this month.

It begins with the D alone, on the principal stop, held for four slow bars: the very note he silenced by hiding the paper there. Then the tune unfolds around it, flute above and pedals walking below, and the D sounds through nearly every bar like a lamp left in a window. The middle is hard. My left hand and my feet must travel in opposite directions.

Dickon Pyle practises too. A long held note shows every unevenness in the wind, and he is learning to pump as smoothly as breathing. The new bellows leather does not hiss. The committee has asked what I mean to play at Midwinter. I said, something old.

volumes.title: December: Midwinter
volumes.text:
On Midwinter Eve the chapel in Tallow Street was full, with a candle in every window and snow on the sills. I knocked once on the organ case. Behind it, Dickon Pyle began to pump.

I played the D alone. A few heads lifted. Nobody in Emberwick under sixty had ever heard that note from this organ, though they could not have said what was different. Then Mr. Thrupp's tune came in around it. I smudged one bar in the hard middle and was forgiven. The last page gathers every stop, trumpet and all, and ends as it began, on the single D fading into the roof.

In the quiet old Mrs. Hale said, quite loudly, “That's Elias.” She had heard him practise it through the wall as a girl. His manuscript hangs framed in the vestry now. The D has other work to do.

volumes.title: The Midwife's Notebook
volumes.text:
I am Mabel Tansy, and I have been midwife in Emberwick for thirty years. I have heard more lullabies through bedroom doors than anyone living and never written one down. This year I shall. My daughter Rose expects her first child at Midwinter, and a grandmother ought to arrive with the right song. I mean to collect eleven and choose. The first is from Mrs. Oram, the baker's wife, who sings at four in the morning while the dough proves.

Sleep, my crumb, the oven's warm,
The loaves are rising slow;
The night is only flour and dark,
And morning's in the dough.

She sings it low, on three notes, in time with her kneading. Babies raised over a bakery, she says, will sleep through anything except silence.

volumes.title: The Fisher's Rocking Song
volumes.text:
At Skarne Haven on the Grey Coast the cradles are rocked by foot. Annet Pellow sits mending nets with both hands, a loop of cord round her ankle, and the cradle swings each time she moves her heel. Her song keeps the same slow pace, rising on the first line and falling on the second, like a boat lifted and set down.

Out goes the tide and in again,
The lamps are on the bay;
The sea that rocks your father's boat
Will rock your cares away.

I am Mabel Tansy, midwife of Emberwick, collecting lullabies this year for a grandchild of my own. Annet had this one from her mother, who had it from hers. She says it works best with real waves behind it, and that inland babies must take it on trust.

volumes.title: The Shepherd's Count
volumes.text:
Not every lullaby belongs to a mother. On a farm in the Northern Fells I heard Will Harker, a shepherd with hands like spades, sing his small son to sleep with a counting song. He holds the child against his chest so that the deep notes are felt as much as heard.

One for the ewe on the fellside steep,
Two for the lamb beside her,
Three for the dog who minds their sleep,
Four for the sky grown wider.

It goes on to ten, each number slower and quieter than the last, and Will makes up the later verses fresh every night. He told me, Mabel Tansy, writing it all down in my notebook, that in two years he has never once reached seven with the boy still awake. Eight, nine and ten, he admits, have never been properly finished.

volumes.title: The Marsh Hush
volumes.text:
In the marsh east of Emberwick the reed-cutters' wives hardly sing at all. Their lullaby is half whispered, with a long shh between the lines that sounds like wind going through the reed beds. Nell Wend showed it to me in a cottage on stilts, with her baby in a rush basket.

Hush, the reeds are saying hush,
The heron's gone to bed;
The frog has folded up his song
And laid it by his head.

There are only two notes in it, a step apart, and you rock on the shh rather than on the words. I am a midwife, and I have collected lullabies all this year for my daughter's coming child. This is the quietest so far. Nell says a loud lullaby is a contradiction, like a hot snowball, and I could not argue with her.

volumes.title: The Miller's Wheel
volumes.text:
Old Mrs. Tranter, the miller's mother at Harrowmill on the river Ember, has sung three generations to sleep with the same song, to the sound of the wheel outside the window.

Round goes the wheel, and the river goes by,
It has nowhere to be but the sea;
And you've nowhere to be but here, my eye,
So go round to sleep with me.

The tune is cleverer than it seems. Its last note is also its first, so the song joins end to end like a hoop and can be sung for an hour without a seam. She sways from foot to foot with it, as slowly as the wheel turns. I wrote it down for my collection, which is meant for my daughter Rose, whose baby comes at Midwinter. Mrs. Tranter's advice was free: never be the first to stop.

volumes.title: The Lamplighter's Verse
volumes.text:
Jem Corbel lights the street lamps of Emberwick, and his daughter's bedtime falls just as he must go out with his ladder. So he sings to her from the doorway with his cap already on.

I've lit the lamp at the end of the lane,
And the lamp by the baker's door;
There's one in the window to light me home,
And you need watch no more.

It is a walking tune, steady and plain, and he sings it getting quieter, as if he were already going away down the street. By the last line he is. His wife says the child is asleep before the gate clicks. I am Mabel Tansy, the midwife, and this is the sixth lullaby in my notebook. I am halfway to the eleven I promised myself, and no nearer knowing which I shall sing to my own grandchild.

volumes.title: A Song Without Words
volumes.text:
Old Mrs. Quillet of Kettle Row, Emberwick, has been deaf for twenty years and has raised, by her own count, nine grandchildren through their worst nights. Her lullaby has no words, and she has never heard it.

She hums three notes down and three notes back up, over and over. With it she pats the baby's back: two soft pats and a rest, two pats and a rest, at the pace of a slow heart. She feels the hum in her own chest and the child feels it through her shoulder.

I, Mabel Tansy, sat and watched a furious infant go quiet in under five minutes. I could not write this one down as a verse, so I have drawn the pats as dots. Half of any lullaby is the hand, I think now. Perhaps rather more than half.

volumes.title: Tilly Sings to Her Doll
volumes.text:
The eighth lullaby in my collection comes from a singer aged five. Tilly Oram, the Emberwick baker's youngest, was putting a rag doll to bed in a flour bin and did not know that the midwife was listening at the door.

Go to sleep, you've had your tea,
You've had your wash, you've had your say;
If you don't sleep then nor shall we,
And I've got things to do today.

She sang it firmly, on one note, shaking the doll in time. I recognised every word. It is what a tired mother says, set down faithfully by the one person who hears it nightly. A lullaby does not have to be poetry to be true. I have promised Tilly never to tell her mother where I got it. The doll, I am told, slept perfectly.

volumes.title: The Song of the Road
volumes.text:
A family of travelling tinsmiths camps each spring on the Lowlands road outside Netherby, and the mother, Seffy Lovage, sings in the rhythm of the van. Her lullaby jogs along like a horse at a walk, with a small dip in every line where a wheel might find a rut.

The road is long, the wheels are round,
The horse knows where to go;
The stars are nails in a big dark roof,
And home is where we slow.

Her children, she told me, cannot sleep in a house. The bed keeps too still. I am Mabel Tansy, midwife of Emberwick, and I wrote her song into my notebook by the light of their fire. She would take nothing for it. A lullaby is the one thing a traveller can give away, she said, and still have when she leaves.

volumes.title: A Lullaby for the Old
volumes.text:
Lullabies are not only for babies. Mr. Tolliver of Mill Street, Emberwick, is ninety-one and sleeps badly, and his daughter Agnes sits by him at night and sings the song he once sang to her.

The day was long, you carried it far,
Now set it by the door;
The kettle's off, the gate is barred,
There's nothing to do more.

She sings it very slowly and a little flat, which is how he always sang it, and holds his hand through the last line. He joins in on the word door. I have attended a great many beginnings in thirty years as a midwife. This one I collected at the other end, and I am glad I did. It is the tenth in my notebook. My own grandchild is due in six weeks, and I still have not chosen.

volumes.title: The Lullaby That Failed
volumes.text:
The schoolmaster of Emberwick, Mr. Vole, has twin boys who will sleep to no song whatever. He borrowed my notebook and tried all ten lullabies on them in one evening. They enjoyed the concert and asked for more. What works, he found by accident, is arithmetic, chanted in a flat and patient voice.

Seven sevens are forty-nine,
Eight eights are sixty-four;
Nine nines are eighty-one, and then
There isn't any more.

They seldom last beyond the sixes. So a lullaby, I now think, is anything said kindly and without hurry. That makes eleven in my book, and my daughter Rose's baby is due within the fortnight. I, Mabel Tansy, who set out to choose the right song, have read all eleven through twice tonight and cannot choose at all.

volumes.title: The Twelfth, Unplanned
volumes.text:
My granddaughter was born at four on Midwinter morning, in Emberwick, with snow against the door. I was not the midwife. The young one from Netherby did the work, and I boiled kettles, badly. Then Rose handed me the baby, and I opened my mouth to sing one of my eleven collected lullabies. What came out was none of them.

Eleven songs I brought for you,
And every one has flown;
So here's a twelfth, made up just now,
And it is yours alone.

I cannot tell you the tune. It was whatever my voice did. She slept. Her name is Ivy. So this notebook holds twelve lullabies after all. Eleven belong to the houses where I heard them, and I have only borrowed those. The twelfth belongs to Ivy. I am leaving the book on Rose's shelf, with blank pages at the back.

volumes.title: A Borrowed March
volumes.text:
I am Horatio Bunce, bandmaster of the Emberwick Town Band: four cornets, two horns, a euphonium, two trombones, a bass, two drums, and a fiddle and flute who join us for dances.

For sixty years this band has marched to the Netherby Quickstep, a tune borrowed from the next town and never returned. It is a sound march, two beats to the bar and a hundred and twenty paces to the minute, with the bass drum falling on every left foot. But it is not ours.

This January the mayor stopped me outside the Market Hall. Charter Day falls in September, three hundred years since Emberwick was made a town, and she wants us to parade to a march of our own. I said yes before I had thought. I have never written a note that was not someone else's first.

volumes.title: The Reel Called Kettle Row
volumes.text:
A reel is a quick dance tune in two halves of eight bars, each half played twice, and the whole thing repeated until the dancers give in. In the Emberwick Town Band the fiddle and the flute carry the tune. The brass keep underneath, the bass on the beat and the horns answering off it, which bandsmen call the oom and the pah.

Our oldest reel is named for Kettle Row, the tinsmiths' street. It is full of repeated notes, three and four together, like small hammers at work.

I am the bandmaster, and I am supposed to be writing the town a march by September. Last night I finished sixteen bars and played them to Mrs. Bunce on the cornet. She listened kindly. Then she said it was the Netherby Quickstep, upside down. She was right. I have burnt it.

volumes.title: How Fast Emberwick Walks
volumes.text:
Most marches go at a hundred and twenty paces a minute. That suits a flat parade ground. Emberwick's High Street climbs all the way from the river to the Market Hall, and for sixty years the Town Band has reached the top too breathless to hold a note in tune.

So before writing a bar of the new town march, I took my watch and stood by the pump for a morning, counting feet. The baker climbs the hill at a hundred and four. The lamplighter manages ninety-six. Schoolchildren, late, do a hundred and thirty. Most people, left to themselves, go up at about a hundred and eight.

That is my first decision as a composer. The Emberwick march will go at a hundred and eight paces a minute, the speed this town really walks. I still have no tune. But I know how fast it is.

volumes.title: The Miller's Reel
volumes.text:
We played for the spring dance at Harrowmill, up the river Ember, where they always ask for the Miller's Reel. It has the rhythm of the mill wheel inside it, two quick notes and a heavy one, over and over, and the dancers stamp on the heavy one until the floor complains.

Our new side drummer is Posy Larkin, who is eleven and took the drum over from her grandfather. She is neat and quick, and she hurries. I have told her to listen to the bass drum as if it were her own breathing.

Walking home I could not get the wheel out of my head, and I stopped fighting it. The march I am writing for Emberwick now has an opening: the side drum alone, three knocks and a rest, twice. It is not a tune yet. It is a knock at the door.

volumes.title: A Slow March
volumes.text:
Once a year, in May, the Emberwick Town Band plays a slow march, when the oldest members of the guilds walk from the bridge to the Market Hall. It goes at about sixty-five paces a minute, and it is the hardest thing we do.

In a quick march, small faults are gone before anyone hears them. In a slow one, every wobble stands in the open. The long notes use up a player's whole breath, so we stagger our breathing, each taking air at a different moment, and the sound never breaks.

I am Horatio Bunce, bandmaster, and my own march for the town still has no melody. I have a speed and a drumbeat. I have tried forty tunes, and each one turned out to belong to somebody else. Mr. Gant, our euphonium, says a tune cannot be hunted. It can only be overheard.

volumes.title: The Ferryman's Whistle
volumes.text:
I crossed the river Ember on the ferry this week, on band business, and heard my march.

Job Hale the ferryman whistles as he pushes off from the bank. It is always the same five notes: up a step, up a leap, then down three like a man coming downstairs. He does not know he does it. His father whistled it on the same ferry. It belongs to nobody but the river, and I wrote it on my shirt cuff before we reached the far side.

Those five notes are now the opening phrase of the Emberwick march. The rest came within the week, as if it had been waiting. The phrase is answered by itself, lower down, and then climbs to the top of the cornets' reach. Sixteen bars. I played them to Mrs. Bunce. She did not mention Netherby at all.

volumes.title: Trio, the Quiet Middle
volumes.text:
Every proper march has a trio. It is the middle section, softer than the rest, set in a key four notes higher, with a smoother tune. The mellow instruments take it, the horns and the euphonium, while the cornets rest their lips. Afterwards the first tune returns, louder, and seems all the better for the holiday.

I am Horatio Bunce, writing a march for Emberwick's Charter Day, and I wanted a trio that did not march at all. I found it by accident. I played our old reel, Kettle Row, at half its speed, and there was a second tune hiding inside it, calm and broad. It was like finding a walking stick inside an umbrella.

So the town's march will carry the town's reel in its middle. I doubt whether anyone will notice. The tinsmiths might.

volumes.title: The Reel of Three Corners
volumes.text:
At midsummer the Emberwick Town Band plays for dancing on the green from the back of a hay cart. The favourite is the Reel of Three Corners, danced in sets of three, with the fiddle and flute leading and the brass let loose on the last time through.

Dancers always push a reel faster. The band's art is to give way slowly. This year it was Posy Larkin, our eleven-year-old drummer, who held us steady when I did not.

I wish my new march had gone as well. At its first rehearsal the cornets cracked on the top note in bar twelve, every time. Mrs. Ottery, our bass, pointed out that I had given her one note for sixteen bars. She said she would fall asleep and then off the kerb. I have gone home to write it again.

volumes.title: Writing Out the Parts
volumes.text:
A march for fourteen players must be written out fourteen times, and not in the same key. A cornet's written note sounds one step lower than it looks, so its part is set a step higher than the tune really is. One slip of the pen puts a horn wrong for the whole march.

I have mended what the first rehearsal of the Emberwick march showed up. The tune now sits a note lower, to spare the cornets. The bass has a walking part that strides down the scale while the tune climbs. The euphonium has a melody of its own, running underneath.

I copied by lamplight for eleven nights while Mrs. Bunce ruled the lines. On the last night I found the second horn, at bar twenty, playing in another march altogether. It had sounded perfectly well in my head.

volumes.title: The Rival from Netherby
volumes.text:
Mr. Septimus Crake, bandmaster of Netherby, wrote to say he had heard that Emberwick was giving up his town's Quickstep after sixty years, and that he was wounded. A second letter followed. He would bring his band to our Charter Day, so that we might be compared.

So the Emberwick Town Band has been practising the countermarch, which is how a band turns round in a street without stopping. The front rank wheels about and marches back through the ranks behind, and each rank follows in turn, playing all the while.

We tried it in Mill Lane. The trombones need a yard of clear air in front of them. The bass drummer cannot see over his drum. There were two collisions and a dented horn. I, Horatio Bunce, have composed a march. I had forgotten we must also walk.

volumes.title: Rehearsal in the Rain
volumes.text:
A week before Charter Day we took the new march up Emberwick High Street in the rain, to see whether it would hold. Posy Larkin gave her three knocks and a rest on the side drum. The cornets came in with the ferryman's five notes. People opened their doors.

At a hundred and eight paces a minute, the hill did not beat us. For the first time in sixty years the band reached the Market Hall with breath to spare.

One fault remained. We arrived twelve bars before the march did, and stood playing at the steps like guests who will not leave. A street is not a fixed length of music. So I have borrowed the old signal: two double taps on the bass drum mean finish at the next full close. I, the composer, find that the drum has the last word.

volumes.title: The Emberwick March
volumes.text:
On Charter Day the Netherby band played their old Quickstep down the High Street, very smartly, and then the Emberwick Town Band played the new march up it.

Posy Larkin's three knocks sounded alone in the quiet. Then four cornets turned the corner with five notes, and Job Hale the ferryman, standing on the kerb, looked behind him to see who was whistling. At the trio the tinsmiths of Kettle Row began to nod. By the second time through, the children behind us were marching at exactly a hundred and eight.

Two double taps, and we finished on the top step of the Market Hall. Mr. Crake of Netherby shook my hand and asked for a copy of the parts. The mayor asked what it was called. It is in the band book now, between the borrowed march and the reels, under its own name.
